summary:
In *Röman v. Finland* (Application no. 13072/05, judgment 29 January 2013), the applicant, Mirja Anneli Röman, was born in Finland in 1954 out of wedlock and initially bore her mother’s maiden name. In 1954 her mother and biological father concluded a child-support agreement verified by social services. In 1956 her mother married another man, and in 1961 the applicant’s surname was changed to that of her mother’s husband. The spouses agreed that the biological father would never be mentioned. Although the church register—which served as the official population register until 1993—listed the mother’s husband as the applicant’s stepfather, the later State population register recorded him as her father.

The applicant eventually began to question her biological origins. In 2001 she discovered the church-register discrepancy and located a copy of the child-support agreement in social-services archives, which enabled her to identify her biological father. On 25 September 2002 the State population-register information was corrected. On 6 February 2003 she initiated paternity proceedings against her biological father in the Vantaa District Court, claiming she had only learned in December 2001 that her mother’s husband was not her biological father.

The domestic courts dismissed her claim as time-barred. Under the Implementing Act of the Paternity Act, which entered into force on 1 October 1976, paternity proceedings for children born before that date had to be initiated within five years—by 1 October 1981. The law also barred proceedings after the putative father’s death. The District Court found that the applicant had been an adult during the five-year period and could have questioned her mother or checked the church register. It held that applying the time-limit did not violate the Constitution or the Convention. The Helsinki Court of Appeal upheld that decision on the same grounds. On 12 October 2004 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. In 2005 the Deputy Parliamentary Ombudsman considered that the national courts had acted within their margin of appreciation. In 2007 a private DNA test showed 99.99% certainty that the identified man was her biological father; he died in 2008.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Under Article 8, she complained that the absolute five-year time-limit prevented her from having her biological father’s paternity legally established, interfering with her private life and her right to know her origins and identity. She argued that she had no real opportunity to bring proceedings within the limitation period because her family had concealed the truth and official records were inconsistent; she only discovered the relevant facts in 2001. Under Article 14, she alleged discrimination because children born after the Paternity Act entered into force could seek establishment of paternity without the same five-year time-limit or the bar following the father’s death. She was thus treated differently on grounds of birth status, date of birth, and origin. The Government relied on legal certainty and protection of putative fathers, but the case raised whether the rigid transitional rule struck a fair balance, particularly given modern DNA evidence.

Her mother and biological father concluded a verified child-support agreement. In 1956 the mother married another man, and in 1961 the applicant’s name was changed to her mother’s husband’s. The family agreed that the biological father would never be mentioned, and the applicant grew up with her mother’s husband registered as her father. In 2001 she discovered in church records that he was listed as her stepfather, while the State population register listed him as her father. She located the child-support agreement and her biological father. In 2002 the population register was corrected.

The legal obstacle arose from the Paternity Act, which entered into force on 1 October 1976. Its Implementing Act allowed paternity proceedings for children born before that date only if initiated within five years, i.e. by 1 October 1981; no claim could be examined after the putative father’s death. No such time-limit applied to children born after the Act. In February 2003 the applicant began paternity proceedings. The Vantaa District Court dismissed the claim as time-barred, finding that during the five-year period she was an adult and could have questioned her mother or checked the church register. The Helsinki Court of Appeal upheld that decision, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. The Deputy Parliamentary Ombudsman later considered that the courts had acted within their margin of appreciation. A private DNA test in 2007 showed 99.99% certainty that the man was her biological father; he died in 2008.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Articles 8 and 14. Under Article 8, she argued that the State’s refusal to allow paternity to be established prevented her from knowing and legally confirming her biological origins, an essential part of private life and identity. She stressed that she could not have complied with the five-year deadline because, for reasons beyond her control, she did not know until 2001 that her mother’s husband was not her biological father; the family never discussed the issue and official records were misleading. During the limitation period she had no reason or interest to challenge paternity. Under Article 14, she complained of discrimination: children born before the Paternity Act were subject to the five-year limit, while children born afterwards were not, and the rule operated regardless of when the child learned the truth.

Domestic law recognised equality and private life under the Constitution. The Paternity Act aimed to improve the position of children born out of wedlock. The transitional five-year limit was originally justified by legal certainty, protection of putative fathers, and concerns about evidence. The Supreme Court had generally applied it strictly, though it allowed an exception. In KKO 2012:11, the Supreme Court in plenum later found that applying the time-limit could evidently conflict with the Constitution and Article 8 where legal or factual reasons beyond the child’s control prevented timely proceedings; DNA testing had reduced the original evidentiary justification, and knowing one’s biological origin is central to private life. It therefore left the time-limit inapplicable and confirmed paternity in that case.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 8 and considered it unnecessary to examine Article 14 separately. The key issue was the rigidity of the transitional time-limit, which failed to accommodate the applicant’s late discovery and made legal establishment of her biological father impossible.

case_name: CASE OF KOVIĆ AND OTHERS v. SERBIA
summary:
**Case: Ković and Others v. Serbia**  
**Applications nos. 39611/08, 50121/13 and 2490/14**  
**Judgment: 4 April 2017 (Third Section, Committee)**

The case concerned three Serbian nationals—Nikola Ković, Zoran Ranković and Ivan Bojanić—who complained under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that various administrative and civil proceedings involving them had exceeded a reasonable time. Their applications were lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 July 2008, 5 June 2013 and 16 December 2013, respectively.

On 18 December 2014, the Court communicated to the Serbian Government the applicants’ complaints concerning the length of administrative and civil proceedings. The remainder of the applications was declared inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The Government objected to the case being examined by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are set out in the appended table.

**Nikola Ković** (born 21 July 1941) had proceedings that began in October 2001 and on 9 November 2001. Those proceedings were still pending at the time of the table. Since 3 March 2004, when the Convention entered into force in respect of Serbia, the total length was 10 years and 8 months before one level of jurisdiction. Ković obtained a decision of the Constitutional Court of Serbia finding a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time. Under the regulations then applicable, the Constitutional Court established his right to seek compensation for non-pecuniary damage before the Commission for Damage Compensation. He submitted his compensation request to the Commission on 26 December 2010, but had received no response by the time of the case. This unresolved compensation procedure is a significant fact concerning the effectiveness of the domestic remedy after the Constitutional Court’s finding.

**Zoran Ranković** (born 3 September 1954), represented by Mile Petković, had proceedings that started on 25 July 2002 and ended on 18 May 2012. Since 3 March 2004, the total length was 8 years and 2 months across two levels of jurisdiction. The Constitutional Court found a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time and awarded him a certain sum in respect of non-pecuniary damage.

**Ivan Bojanić** (born 22 April 1978), represented by Dragan Radin, had proceedings that began on 11 March 2004 and ended on 25 May 2011. Since 3 March 2004, the total length was 7 years and 2 months across two levels of jurisdiction. The Constitutional Court also found a violation and awarded him compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

In essence, the applicants’ alleged violation was the excessive length of administrative and civil proceedings contrary to the reasonable-time requirement of Article 6 § 1. The central factual elements are the long durations after 3 March 2004, the number of judicial levels involved, and the prior Constitutional Court decisions. For Ković, the key additional fact is that his subsequent compensation request remained unanswered; for Ranković and Bojanić, the key facts are that the Constitutional Court found violations and awarded them non-pecuniary damages. The Court was therefore called upon to assess whether the length of the proceedings breached Article 6 § 1 in light of those domestic findings and remedies.

case_name: CASE OF HORNCASTLE AND OTHERS v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary:
In *Horncastle and Others v. the United Kingdom* (App. no. 4184/10, 16 Dec. 2014), four British nationals alleged that admitting absent witnesses’ statements at their trials made the proceedings unfair under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d), particularly the right to cross-examine witnesses. The case concerned two separate prosecutions.

First, Horncastle and Blackmore were charged with causing grievous bodily harm with intent to P.R. In May 2005 P.R., a registered alcoholic, was attacked in his flat by three men; he later died in July 2006. Before death, he made a police statement identifying “Horncastle” and describing the others, including a “bigger male” and a man on crutches. The prosecution alleged Horncastle, Blackmore and D. went to P.R.’s flat to recover stolen property; Blackmore was the bigger male and D. the man on crutches. The defence denied involvement and suggested M. was the attacker. Since P.R. had died, the prosecution applied to read his statement under section 116(2)(a) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003. The defence objected that it was unfair: the statement was the only admissible evidence of participation, could not be cross-examined, and was unreliable because P.R. had been drinking, had vague memory, and gave a description not fitting Blackmore. The judge admitted it, finding the statutory condition met and that jury directions could address the disadvantage. Other evidence included admissions of presence, Horncastle removing a television stained with P.R.’s blood, Blackmore stepping over the victim, and forensic evidence. The jury convicted. The Court of Appeal accepted the statement was decisive but found sufficient safeguards; the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

Second, Marquis and Graham were charged with kidnapping H.M. On 1 November 2007, six men entered her home, threatened her with a knife, stole property and kidnapped her, demanding ransom. H.M. made a statement but later retracted it through fear. She then made a video statement saying she was terrified, failed to attend court, and fled. The prosecution applied under section 116(2)(e) to read her statement because she would not testify through fear. The defence argued her fear was not caused by the applicants but largely by police warnings about dangerous men and relocation. The judge found genuine fear and admitted the statement; he declined to admit her partner G.P.’s statement. Other evidence included CCTV of Graham entering the house and driving the stolen car, telephone records linking Marquis to ransom calls, a knife identified by H.M., and hotel evidence. The jury convicted. The Court of Appeal found the statement was not decisive and the trial fair; the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

CASE OF HORNCASTLE AND OTHERS v. THE UNITED KINGDOM (no. 4184/10) concerned four British applicants convicted in separate English criminal trials. Their common allegation was that the admission of absent witnesses’ statements as evidence denied them any opportunity to cross-examine those witnesses, rendering their trials unfair under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention.

In the first case, Mr Horncastle and Mr Blackmore were charged with causing grievous bodily harm with intent to P.R., a registered alcoholic. P.R. was attacked in his flat in May 2005 and suffered extensive injuries. In a police statement dated 3 June 2005, he said he had drunk at least three litres of cider and that his memory was vague. He nevertheless described three attackers, including a “bigger male”, a man on crutches, and a man named Horncastle. P.R. died in July 2006 from an alcohol-related illness. The prosecution applied to read his statement under section 116(2)(a) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 (“CJA”) because the witness was dead. The defence objected under section 78 of PACE, arguing that the statement was the only evidence of participation, inherently unreliable because of P.R.’s intoxication and vague memory, and impossible to test by cross-examination. The judge admitted it. At trial, both applicants admitted going to the flat to recover stolen property, but Horncastle denied seeing an assault, while Blackmore admitted stepping over P.R.’s prostrate body and seeing blood. Other evidence included blood matching P.R. on a television removed by Horncastle, forensic evidence about the attack location, and defence evidence suggesting another man, M., was responsible. The judge gave detailed hearsay directions and reminded the jury of the disadvantages to the defence. They were convicted.

In the second case, Mr Marquis and Mr Graham were charged with kidnapping H.M. on 1 November 2007. Six men entered her home, threatened her with a knife, demanded a ransom, and later released her. H.M. made a police statement describing the incident but did not identify either applicant. The prosecution relied additionally on CCTV showing Graham entering the house, his arrest in the victim’s partner’s stolen car, a knife, telephone records linking Marquis to ransom calls, and evidence that a phone identical to the victim’s was seen in Marquis’s hotel room. H.M. and her partner later retracted their statements, saying they were frightened. Before trial, H.M. failed to attend and fled. The prosecution applied to read her statement under section 116(2)(e) CJA on the ground that she would not give evidence through fear. The defence argued that the fear was not caused by the applicants but by police warnings about dangerous men and relocation. The judge found H.M. genuinely terrified, admitted her statement, but declined to admit the partner’s statement. Marquis and Graham were convicted after directions on the limitations of hearsay.

The domestic courts dismissed appeals. The Court of Appeal accepted that in the first case P.R.’s statement was decisive but found sufficient safeguards; in the second it found the statement was not decisive and other evidence supported conviction. The Supreme Court also dismissed the appeals. Before the European Court, the applicants alleged that admitting these statements rendered their trials unfair because they could not cross-examine the absent witnesses. The ECtHR found no violation, holding that the CJA safeguards and judicial directions provided sufficient counterbalancing measures.

Case of Horncastle and Others v. the United Kingdom (App. no. 4184/10) concerned four British nationals convicted in two separate criminal cases. They alleged that admitting written statements by absent witnesses at their trials breached Article 6 §§1 and 3(d) of the Convention because they had no opportunity to cross-examine those witnesses, making the proceedings unfair.

In the first case, Michael Horncastle and David Blackmore were charged with causing grievous bodily harm with intent to P.R. In May 2005 P.R., a registered alcoholic, was attacked in his flat and suffered extensive injuries. In June 2005 he made a police statement describing the attack. He admitted drinking at least three litres of cider that day, said his memory was vague, but described three attackers: a “bigger male”, a man on crutches, and a third man called “Horncastle”. P.R. died in July 2006 from an alcohol-related illness. The prosecution alleged that Horncastle and Blackmore went with D., the owner of stolen property, to recover it; Blackmore was the “bigger male” and D. was the man on crutches. The defence admitted being present but denied assault, blaming M. The victim’s statement was the only admissible evidence of participation. Over defence objection, the trial judge admitted it under section 116(2)(a) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 because the witness was dead. The judge found admission not unfair and gave detailed hearsay directions. The jury convicted both applicants; the Court of Appeal upheld the convictions.

In the second case, Abijah Marquis and Joseph Graham were charged with kidnapping H.M. In November 2007 masked men entered H.M.’s home, stole property, threatened her with a knife, abducted her, demanded a £100,000 ransom, and threatened to cut off her fingers and toes. H.M. made statements but did not identify any attacker. She later retracted them because she was scared, then gave a video statement saying she was terrified, slept badly, and feared reprisals. She and her partner failed to attend trial; H.M. fled the day before. The prosecution applied to read her statement under section 116(2)(e) CJA 2003 as a witness in fear. The judge admitted it, finding she was genuinely terrified and would rather face arrest than testify, although a police officer’s earlier warnings had contributed to her fear. Other evidence included CCTV of Graham at the house, his arrest in the stolen car with a knife, telephone records linking Marquis to ransom calls, and hotel evidence. Marquis and Graham were convicted of kidnapping; the Court of Appeal upheld.

The applicants argued that using absent witnesses’ statements, especially where sole or decisive, violated their right to examine witnesses and rendered their trials unfair, relying on Al-Khawaja and Tahery. The domestic courts emphasised statutory safeguards: judicial gatekeeping, strict admissibility rules, jury directions, the power to stop a case if hearsay evidence was unconvincing, and other evidence capable of testing reliability. The European Court of Human Rights assessed the fairness of the proceedings as a whole and found no violation of Article 6, accepting that the UK’s hearsay regime contained sufficient counterbalancing safeguards.

case_name: CASE OF CENTRUM FÖR RÄTTVISA v. SWEDEN
summary:
In *Centrum för rättvisa v. Sweden* (Application no. 35252/08), the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights delivered judgment on 25 May 2021. The applicant is a Swedish foundation based in Stockholm that represents clients in Convention-related proceedings, conducts education and research, and participates in public debate on rights. It communicates daily with individuals, organisations and companies in Sweden and abroad by email, telephone and fax, much of that communication being sensitive from a privacy perspective. Because it scrutinises State actors, it claims a risk that its communications have been or will be intercepted and examined through Swedish signals intelligence. It did not bring domestic proceedings, arguing that no effective remedy existed.

The applicant alleged that Swedish legislation and practice on signals intelligence violated Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life and correspondence) and that it lacked an effective remedy, contrary to Article 13.

The relevant Swedish framework is the Foreign Intelligence Act and the Signals Intelligence Act, which entered into force on 1 January 2009 and was amended several times. The National Defence Radio Establishment (FRA) may conduct signals intelligence only for specified foreign-intelligence purposes, including external military threats; international peacekeeping or humanitarian missions; strategic international terrorism or other serious cross-border crime threatening essential national interests; proliferation of weapons of mass destruction; serious external threats to societal infrastructure; foreign conflicts with consequences for international security; foreign intelligence operations against Swedish interests; and actions or intentions of foreign powers of substantial importance to Swedish foreign, security or defence policy. It may not be used to solve ordinary law-enforcement or crime-prevention tasks, though support may be provided.

Cable-based cross-border communications may be transferred to collection points. Purely domestic communications are prohibited and must be destroyed if inadvertently collected. Interception is automated and based on selectors or search terms. Selectors directly relating to a specific natural person may be used only if exceptionally important. Permits are issued by the Foreign Intelligence Court, which must verify compliance, necessity, proportionality, and that the application does not solely target a specific person. Permits are time-limited to a maximum of six months and may be renewed. Urgent permits granted by the FRA must be reviewed by the court.

Safeguards include destruction rules for irrelevant personal data and for protected media sources, attorney-client communications and religious confessions; personal-data processing restrictions; supervision by the Foreign Intelligence Inspectorate, which may order cessation or destruction; a Privacy Protection Council; data protection officers; the Data Protection Authority; and scrutiny by the Parliamentary Ombudsmen and Chancellor of Justice. Persons may be notified if selectors directly related to them were used, but notification can be delayed for secrecy and need not be given where measures concern foreign powers. Individuals may ask the Inspectorate to investigate whether their communications were intercepted and whether this was lawful; may request information from the FRA; may seek correction or destruction of data; may claim damages; and may appeal certain decisions to the Administrative Court.

The Chamber declared the application admissible but found no violation of Article 8 and no need to examine Article 13 separately. The applicant requested referral, and the Grand Chamber granted it. The central alleged violations therefore concern whether the secret signals-intelligence regime, given its scope and secrecy/notification limits, breached Article 8 and whether domestic oversight and remedies were sufficient under Article 13.

*Centrum för rättvisa v. Sweden* is a Grand Chamber judgment of the European Court of Human Rights delivered on 25 May 2021. It supports Swedish foreign, defence and security policy and must concern foreign circumstances. Interception is automated and uses selectors or search terms. Selectors directly relating to a specific natural person may be used only if of exceptional importance for intelligence activities. Safeguards require destruction of irrelevant or privileged data, including attorney-client communications, religious confession information, and anonymous media-source material. Oversight is exercised by the Foreign Intelligence Inspectorate, the Data Protection Authority, the Parliamentary Ombudsmen and the Chancellor of Justice. Individuals may ask the Inspectorate to investigate whether their communications were intercepted and whether the law was followed; they may also request information, correction and damages, but secrecy can prevent notification or disclosure. Notification is required if selectors directly relate to a specific person, but may be delayed or omitted for secrecy reasons and was reportedly never used due to secrecy.

The applicant alleged that the legislation and practice violated Article 8 of the Convention because signals intelligence created a risk of interception of its sensitive communications and lacked adequate safeguards against abuse, especially given the secrecy surrounding the system. It also alleged a violation of Article 13 because it had no effective remedy to challenge the interception or obtain notification.

In *Centrum för rättvisa v. Sweden* (Application no. 35252/08), the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights delivered judgment on 25 May 2021. The applicant is a Swedish foundation based in Stockholm that represents clients in Convention-related proceedings, conducts education and research, and participates in public debate on rights. It communicates daily with individuals, organisations and companies in Sweden and abroad by email, telephone and fax, much of that communication being sensitive from a privacy perspective. Because it scrutinises State actors, it claims a risk that its communications have been or will be intercepted and examined through Swedish signals intelligence. It did not bring domestic proceedings, arguing that no effective remedy existed.

The applicant alleged that Swedish legislation and practice on signals intelligence violated Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private life and correspondence) and that it lacked an effective remedy, contrary to Article 13.

The relevant Swedish framework is the Foreign Intelligence Act and the Signals Intelligence Act, which entered into force on 1 January 2009 and was amended several times. The National Defence Radio Establishment (FRA) may conduct signals intelligence only for specified foreign-intelligence purposes, including external military threats; international peacekeeping or humanitarian missions; strategic international terrorism or other serious cross-border crime threatening essential national interests; proliferation of weapons of mass destruction; serious external threats to societal infrastructure; foreign conflicts with consequences for international security; foreign intelligence operations against Swedish interests; and actions or intentions of foreign powers of substantial importance to Swedish foreign, security or defence policy. It may not be used to solve ordinary law-enforcement or crime-prevention tasks, though support may be provided.

Cable-based cross-border communications may be transferred to collection points. Purely domestic communications are prohibited and must be destroyed if inadvertently collected. Interception is automated and based on selectors or search terms. Selectors directly relating to a specific natural person may be used only if exceptionally important. Permits are issued by the Foreign Intelligence Court, which must verify compliance, necessity, proportionality, and that the application does not solely target a specific person. Permits are time-limited to a maximum of six months and may be renewed. Urgent permits granted by the FRA must be reviewed by the court.

Safeguards include destruction rules for irrelevant personal data and for protected media sources, attorney-client communications and religious confessions; personal-data processing restrictions; supervision by the Foreign Intelligence Inspectorate, which may order cessation or destruction; a Privacy Protection Council; data protection officers; the Data Protection Authority; and scrutiny by the Parliamentary Ombudsmen and Chancellor of Justice. Persons may be notified if selectors directly related to them were used, but notification can be delayed for secrecy and need not be given where measures concern foreign powers. Individuals may ask the Inspectorate to investigate whether their communications were intercepted and whether this was lawful; may request information from the FRA; may seek correction or destruction of data; may claim damages; and may appeal certain decisions to the Administrative Court.

The Chamber declared the application admissible but found no violation of Article 8 and no need to examine Article 13 separately. The applicant requested referral, and the Grand Chamber granted it. The central alleged violations therefore concern whether the secret signals-intelligence regime, given its scope and secrecy/notification limits, breached Article 8 and whether domestic oversight and remedies were sufficient under Article 13.
